p.src: The Course Begins Again with Relativity

u.src: The Course Begins Again with Relativity
en: The Course Begins Again with Relativity

p.src: This quarter returns to classical physics, but not to the Newtonian picture in which space and time are independent and universal. The immediate subjects are special relativity and classical field theory, especially electromagnetism. Quantum mechanics will not be used. The earlier mechanics course supplied the action principle and the Hamiltonian and Lagrangian descriptions; the quantum course supplied its basic principles, although even the harmonic oscillator had to be left for a later return. Light was also largely absent. That omission is now repaired, because light is intrinsically relativistic.

p.src: Most of the class has encountered special relativity before. Nevertheless, a show of hands favors rebuilding it from the beginning. That is the useful choice. The Lorentz transformation should not enter as a formula to memorize. It should emerge because operational measurements of space and time cannot satisfy both Galilean kinematics and the observed law of light propagation.

p.src: Coordinates as physical apparatus

u.src: Coordinates as physical apparatus
en: Coordinates as physical apparatus

p.src: Begin with a Cartesian frame: an origin, three oriented axes, and coordinates $x,y,z$. A concrete realization would fill space with a rigid lattice of meter sticks. To identify an event rather than merely a place, each point of the lattice also carries a clock. An event is then labeled $(x,y,z,t).$ The clocks must be synchronized by some stated procedure; that requirement will soon become the delicate part of the construction.

p.src: A reference frame is a spatial coordinate lattice together with a distributed system of synchronized clocks. An inertial frame is a nonrotating, nonaccelerating frame in which every force-free particle moves at constant velocity.

p.src: Two frames in relative uniform motion assign different coordinates to the same event. A point fixed in the moving frame has a constant coordinate $x'$, even while its unprimed coordinate changes. In Newtonian physics the spatial relation for motion along the $x$-direction is $x'=x-vt.$ The less conspicuous Newtonian assumption is that all well-set watches remain universally synchronized: $t'=t.$

p.src: The principle of relativity

u.src: The principle of relativity
en: The principle of relativity

p.src: Relativity did not begin with Einstein. Galileo and Newton already used the principle that the laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame. Newton’s law $F=ma$, the inverse-square law of gravity, and the Coulomb force do not acquire a new form merely because the laboratory moves uniformly.

p.src: The familiar test is a sealed railroad car. If the train moves smoothly and the windows reveal nothing outside, juggling behaves just as it does in a stationary room. Balls rise, fall, and return to the hand in the ordinary way. An experiment confined to the car cannot reveal its uniform velocity. Acceleration or rotation can be detected internally; uniform translational motion cannot.

p.src:
Einstein adds one physical law to this older principle: light in vacuum propagates at $c \simeq 1.86\times 10^5\ {\rm miles/s}
   \simeq 3.00\times 10^8\ {\rm m/s}.$ If this is a law of nature and the laws are the same in every inertial frame, every inertial observer must measure the same $c$.

x'=0.$

p.src: Ordinary velocity addition is an excellent approximation for slow mechanical motion, but measurements of light do not show the predicted $c-v$ and $c+v$. The transformation law, not the light postulate, must be reconsidered. The central suspect is the apparently innocent statement $t'=t$: it asserts an absolute notion of simultaneity.

p.src: Synchronizing Distant Clocks

u.src: Synchronizing Distant Clocks
en: Synchronizing Distant Clocks

p.src: To say that two clocks at different places show the same time requires an experiment. Place a third observer at their midpoint, with equal distances established by meter sticks. Instruct the two end clocks to emit flashes when each reads noon. If the flashes reach the midpoint together, call the clocks synchronized.

en: To say that two clocks at different places show the same time requires an experiment. Place a third observer at their midpoint, with equal distances established by meter sticks. Instruct the two end clocks to emit flashes when each reads noon. If the flashes reach the midpoint together, call the clocks synchronized.

p.src: This is not a philosophical definition laid over the physics. It is a reproducible operation made from clocks, distances, and light signals.

u.src: This is not a philosophical definition laid over the physics. It is a reproducible operation made from clocks, distances, and light signals.
en: This is not a philosophical definition laid over the physics. It is a reproducible operation made from clocks, distances, and light signals.

p.src: Now let an observer move past the midpoint. The end flashes that arrive together at the stationary midpoint do not arrive together at the moving observer: while the light is in flight, that observer moves toward one flash and away from the other. Events judged simultaneous by the stationary clocks are therefore not simultaneous according to the moving frame’s equally valid synchronization procedure.

p.src: Fred, Mary, and Seymour

u.src: Fred, Mary, and Seymour
en: Fred, Mary, and Seymour

p.src: Let Fred occupy $x=vt$, Mary occupy $x=vt+1$, and Seymour occupy $x=vt+2$. At the origin $O$, Fred sends a right-moving light signal to Mary. Seymour sends a left-moving signal so that the two flashes reach Mary at the same event $a$. By the moving frame’s midpoint synchronization rule, Seymour’s emission event $b$ is simultaneous with Fred’s emission at $O$. The line through $O$ and $b$ is therefore $t'=0$.

p.src: The event $a$ lies on both $x=t$ and $x=vt+1.$ Consequently, $t_a=x_a=\frac{1}{1-v}.$

u.src: The event $a$ lies on both $x=t$ and $x=vt+1.$ Consequently, $t_a=x_a=\frac{1}{1-v}.$
en: The event $a$ lies on both $x=t$ and $x=vt+1.$ Consequently, $t_a=x_a=\frac{1}{1-v}.$

p.src:
The left-moving light ray through $a$ obeys $x+t=x_a+t_a=\frac{2}{1-v}.$ Event $b$ also lies on Seymour’s worldline, $x-vt=2.$ Solving  and  gives $\begin{aligned}
t_b&=\frac{2v}{1-v^2},\\
x_b&=\frac{2}{1-v^2}.
\end{aligned}$ The slope of the line from $O$ to $b$ is therefore $\frac{t_b}{x_b}=v,$ so the moving simultaneity line is $t=vx,
\qquad
t'=0.$

p.src: Deriving the Lorentz Transformation

u.src: Deriving the Lorentz Transformation
en: Deriving the Lorentz Transformation

p.src:
The condition $x'=0$ on $x=vt$ requires $x'$ to contain the factor $x-vt$. Likewise, $t'=0$ on $t=vx$ requires the factor $t-vx$. Homogeneity of spacetime makes the transformation linear, so write $\begin{aligned}
x'&=(x-vt)f(v),\\
t'&=(t-vx)g(v).
\end{aligned}$

The condition $x'=0$ on $x=vt$ requires $x'$ to contain the factor $x-vt$. Likewise, $t'=0$ on $t=vx$ requires the factor $t-vx$. Homogeneity of spacetime makes the transformation linear, so write $\begin{aligned}

en:
The condition $x'=0$ on $x=vt$ requires $x'$ to contain the factor $x-vt$. Likewise, $t'=0$ on $t=vx$ requires the factor $t-vx$. Homogeneity of spacetime makes the transformation linear, so write $\begin{aligned}
x'&=(x-vt)f(v),\\
t'&=(t-vx)g(v).
\end{aligned}$

p.src: Reciprocity fixes the scale

u.src: Reciprocity fixes the scale
en: Reciprocity fixes the scale

p.src:
There is no distinguished really moving inertial frame. If the primed frame moves at $v$ relative to the unprimed frame, the unprimed frame moves at $-v$ relative to the primed one. The inverse map must therefore have the same form with the sign of $v$ reversed: $\begin{aligned}
x&=(x'+vt')f(v),\\
t&=(t'+vx')f(v).
\end{aligned}$

p.src: Restoring Ordinary Units

u.src: Restoring Ordinary Units
en: Restoring Ordinary Units

p.src:
Dimensional analysis restores ordinary units. The denominator can depend only on the dimensionless ratio $v^2/c^2$, while $vx$ in the time equation must become $vx/c^2$: $\begin{aligned}
x'&=\gamma(x-vt),&
t'&=\gamma\left(t-\frac{vx}{c^2}\right),
\\
\gamma&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}.
\end{aligned}$ The inverse transformation is $\begin{aligned}
x&=\gamma(x'+vt'),&
t&=\gamma\left(t'+\frac{vx'}{c^2}\right).
\end{aligned}$

p.src:
For $v\ll c$, $\gamma=1+\frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2}+O\!\left(\frac{v^4}{c^4}\right),$ and the transformation reduces to $x'\approx x-vt,
\qquad
t'\approx t.$ At terrestrial speeds the ratios are usually tiny, explaining the success of Newtonian kinematics. Near $c$, the corrections become large.

For $v\ll c$, $\gamma=1+\frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2}+O\!\left(\frac{v^4}{c^4}\right),$ and the transformation reduces to $x'\approx x-vt,
\qquad
t'\approx t.$ At terrestrial speeds the ratios are usually tiny, explaining the success of Newtonian kinematics. Near $c$, the corrections become large.

p.src: Length means the separation of the two endpoints measured at the same time in the frame doing the measurement. It does not mean the apparent angular size of a photographed object, because light-travel delays introduce a separate optical problem.

p.src:
Let a rod be at rest in the unprimed frame with endpoints $x=0,
\qquad
x=1.$ The primed observer measures the endpoint events on a single primed simultaneity slice, say $t'=0$. At the far endpoint $x=1$, $t'=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t=\frac{vx}{c^2}.$ Temporarily returning to $c=1$, this event has $t=v$, and $x'=\frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
   =\frac{1-v^2}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
   =\sqrt{1-v^2}.$

p.src:
Now follow a clock at rest in the primed frame. Along its worldline, $x'=0.$ Compare the event at which it reads $t'=1$ with the origin. The inverse transformation gives $t=\gamma\left(t'+\frac{vx'}{c^2}\right)=\gamma.$ Thus one unit of elapsed time on the moving clock corresponds to $\gamma$ units of unprimed coordinate time: $\Delta t=\gamma\,\Delta\tau,
\qquad
\Delta\tau=\frac{\Delta t}{\gamma}.$

p.src: The effect concerns every physical clock, not merely a mechanism labeled as one. A wristwatch, an atomic transition, metabolism, and biological aging all follow the same proper time. A cheap watch bought on a New York street would not escape relativity by being a poor Rolex; it might keep inaccurate time, but whatever process it uses is still subject to the same kinematics.

p.src: The time-dilation diagram looks perverse if it is read with Euclidean geometry. The slanted path seems like a hypotenuse, yet it carries less proper time than the vertical path. The resolution is not a trick in the algebra. Spacetime has a different metric.

p.src:
In a Euclidean plane, a rotation changes $x$ and $y$ but preserves $x'^2+y'^2=x^2+y^2.$ It is natural to test whether a Lorentz transformation preserves $t^2+x^2$. It does not. In units $c=1$, $\begin{aligned}
t'^2
&=\frac{t^2-2vtx+v^2x^2}{1-v^2},\\
x'^2
&=\frac{x^2-2vtx+v^2t^2}{1-v^2}.\end{aligned}$ Adding leaves the wrong coefficients. Subtracting instead cancels the mixed terms and gives $\begin{aligned}
t'^2-x'^2
&=
\frac{t^2-2vtx+v^2x^2-x^2+2vtx-v^2t^2}{1-v^2}\\
&=t^2-x^2.
\end{aligned}$

p.src:
For two events on the worldline of a clock, choose the clock’s rest frame. There $\Delta x'=0$, so invariance gives $c^2\Delta\tau^2
=c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2,$ or $\Delta\tau
=\sqrt{\Delta t^2-\frac{\Delta x^2}{c^2}}.$ This is the actual time recorded by the clock between the two events.

p.src:
The light rays divide spacetime into three invariant classes: $\begin{aligned}
c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2&>0
&&\text{timelike},\\
c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2&=0
&&\text{null},\\
c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2&<0
&&\text{spacelike}.\end{aligned}$ A physical clock can connect timelike-separated events, and the positive interval determines its proper time. No subluminal object can connect spacelike-separated events. For a spacelike pair one may choose a frame in which the events are simultaneous and define the proper distance $\ell_{\rm proper}
=\sqrt{\Delta x^2-c^2\Delta t^2}.$

p.src: Lorentz Symmetry and Its Historical Meaning

u.src: Lorentz Symmetry and Its Historical Meaning
en: Lorentz Symmetry and Its Historical Meaning

p.src: Einstein’s route was tied closely to electromagnetism. According to his later recollection, already as a teenager he wondered what would happen if he chased a light wave. Galilean velocity subtraction would make the wave appear stationary, but Maxwell’s equations have no corresponding frozen oscillatory light wave in vacuum. That conflict pointed to the kinematics, not to a peculiar mechanical property of measuring rods.

p.src: Maxwell’s equations are invariant under Lorentz transformations rather than Galilean ones. Lorentz and FitzGerald had already found related contraction formulas while retaining an ether and interpreting contraction as a dynamical deformation caused by motion through it. On that view the effect might have been an approximate material response with further corrections.

p.src: Einstein’s decisive step was to make the relativity principle and invariant light speed exact kinematic principles. Length contraction and time dilation then apply to every suitable rod and clock because they express the geometry relating inertial frames, not a special force exerted by an ether. The next task is to formulate particle motion inside this geometry.
